extracted.intended_audience: academics, constitutional-law practitioners, agency attorneys, policymakers, and courts considering First Amendment issues for government social media
extracted.subtask_short: agency social media First Amendment analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Applying public forum and government-speech doctrines to federal agency use of social media and interactive agency websites, and identifying permissible content- and viewpoint-related restrictions on public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government intent to open a forum (Perry test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the government has 'expressly dedicated' property or a site to expressive activity — government intent is a central factor in classifying fora (Perry Educ. Ass’n v. Perry Local Educators’ Ass’n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts often permit the government to define very specific parameters for acceptable expression; the Perry test allows the government to argue a forum was intended for particular speakers/topics. Justice Kennedy criticized overreliance on intent and advocated for an objective inquiry, but lower courts frequently use intent to narrow forum scope. The presence of an express statement of intent (e.g., the President’s Open Government Memorandum urging agencies to use social media) supports finding a forum opened by government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical use as a forum factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a location has been historically used for expressive purposes (traditional public forum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If historical use demonstrates a physical location was used for expressive purposes, it is classified as a traditional public forum and receives the most rigorous protections. Because the Internet and social media lack long historical approbation, they are unlikely to be treated as traditional public fora absent strong arguments; Justice Kennedy has suggested physical similarities can matter in extending traditional-forum status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predominance of private vs. government speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether government or private speech predominates on the agency-operated site; this influences whether the public forum doctrine or government-speech doctrine applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If private speech predominates on a site effectively controlled by the government, public forum analysis is likely most appropriate. The task is to determine whether government or private speech predominates; many agency social media sites are described as 'agency sponsored,' which indicates government role in operating the sites and supports public forum analysis when private speech predominates.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-action principle and private platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether private platforms (Facebook, Twitter, ISPs) can be treated as state actors for First Amendment constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that ISPs or private platforms assume state-action roles (e.g., plaintiffs seeking heightened First Amendment protections from ISPs) have generally failed. State action need not be invoked when the government itself acts to open, operate, or regulate a site; where the government is affirmatively opening and regulating a site, First Amendment constraints on the government apply regardless of private ownership of the underlying platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy to leasing space / 'agency sponsored' characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating agency presence on private platforms as the government leasing or renting space to invite private speech for public purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies (leasing space for town meetings, GSA leasing offices) support applying public-forum principles even on private platforms; sites described as 'agency sponsored' indicate government control sufficient to consider public forum protections. Practical implication: agencies should address their relationship with the provider (e.g., terms of service) to clarify that the site functions as a public space for First Amendment purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of public-forum doctrine to intangible/means-of-communication fora
rubrics_metrics.description: Precedent supports applying public-forum principles to non-spatial or 'metaphysical' fora (Cornelius, Rosenberger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have applied the public forum doctrine to 'means of communication' (employee charity drive) and funds/activity mechanisms; given these precedents, it is reasonable to conclude public forum doctrine could be extended to social media sites, especially given Web 2.0's interactive character within the Internet's 'vast democratic fora.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Incompatibility analysis (compatibility with forum's ordinary activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the method/content of expression is 'incompatible with the normal activity of a place at a particular time' (Grayned incompatibility test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used, incompatibility analysis asks if expression conflicts with the forum’s ordinary activity or purpose; intent is a determining factor in incompatibility analyses. For agency social media opened for communicative purposes (e.g., per Open Government Memorandum), finding speech 'incompatible' with that goal would be tautological unless the speech truly conflicts with the forum's core purpose (safety, order, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum classification and corresponding scrutiny levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify forum type — traditional, designated, limited/public, or non-public — because each classification determines permissible restrictions and scrutiny applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional and designated public fora: content-based restrictions are subject to strict scrutiny. Limited public forum: the government may reserve the forum for certain groups/topics; viewpoint discrimination is strictly scrutinized, but subject-matter limitations are reviewed under intermediate scrutiny (they must be viewpoint neutral and reasonable in light of the forum's purpose). Non-public fora: broader government control is allowed. The article concludes agency social media are 'likely a limited public forum,' which allows some permissible restrictions but requires protection of First Amendment rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content discrimination: viewpoint vs. subject-matter distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Content discrimination covers viewpoint and subject-matter discrimination; viewpoint discrimination is the most suspect and generally triggers strict scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viewpoint discrimination (regulating perspective/opinion/ideology) must meet strict scrutiny. Subject-matter restrictions (regulating topic) are reviewed under intermediate scrutiny in limited fora — they must be viewpoint neutral and reasonable relative to the forum's purpose. The Court's conception of content discrimination embraces both subject-matter and viewpoint discrimination; agencies must avoid treating viewpoint-based exclusions as subject-matter rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to define topical scope and consistent application
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies that establish a limited public forum should explicitly state what topics are permissible and apply rules consistently to avoid converting subject-matter rules into covert viewpoint discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department of State (example) will not post comments that are 'clearly off-topic' but provides no definition; lack of clear, consistently applied topical definitions invites legal challenge. Removing obviously off-topic comments is permissible, but grey areas require careful judgment and consistent moderation; failing to moderate consistently may open later restrictions to strict scrutiny. Agencies may consider moving irrelevant comments to an 'off-topic' category rather than complete deletion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civility codes must be narrow, objective, definite, and viewpoint neutral
rubrics_metrics.description: Civility or comment policies (e.g., requiring respect, prohibiting 'vulgar' or 'objectionable' content) must satisfy First Amendment constraints: they must be sufficiently narrow, objective, and definite, and viewpoint neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague standards ('otherwise objectionable', 'vulgar', 'offensive', 'incites hate') chill speech and function as prior restraints; 'narrow, objective, and definite standards' are required. Banning profanity may be sufficiently objective, but agencies must apply such bans carefully because prohibiting particular words risks suppressing ideas that can be communicated only with strong language. A civility policy is subject to intermediate scrutiny in a limited public forum (reasonable re-purpose and viewpoint neutrality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding covert viewpoint discrimination when enforcing subject-matter rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must be vigilant that subject-matter exclusions are not pretexts for removing disfavored viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts are alert to covert viewpoint discrimination dressed as subject-matter restrictions. Example: removing 'to hell with the Secretary’s policy' as 'off-topic' would likely constitute unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination. Agencies must retain topical comments even if crude, and remove off-topic comments regardless of eloquence, but must not use topic rules to censor viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational/resource considerations for moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: The time and personnel required to implement and enforce subject-matter or civility restrictions may be significant and affect reasonableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcing topical or civility restrictions may absorb agency resources. Even if moderating consumes staff time, it may still be 'reasonable' if aligned with the forum purpose. Agencies should weigh resource burdens and consider less intrusive approaches (e.g., categorizing off-topic content instead of deleting). Consistency in practice is critical to withstand legal scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government speech vs. public-forum choice in mixed/hybrid contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'mixed' or 'hybrid' speech (private speech on government-operated platforms), courts may apply either the public forum doctrine or government-speech analysis, depending on context and precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Garcetti (private speech by public employees treated as government speech) and Forbes (agency-run media treated as public forum) illustrate inconsistent lower-court approaches. Choice of doctrinal frame profoundly affects permissible restrictions; practitioners should analyze whether the challenged content is better characterized as government speech or private expression on a government forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms-of-service agreements and clarifying First Amendment expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies operating on private platforms should consider amending terms-of-service agreements to make clear that government-operated pages are treated as public spaces where First Amendment protections apply to public comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because platforms like Facebook have their own comment policies (sometimes providing more speech protection than some agencies), agencies should negotiate or amend agreements to clarify responsibilities and to assert that agency-operated pages function as public fora for First Amendment purposes; this reduces later conflict about whether platform policy or governmental moderation controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow, objective standards to avoid prior restraint/ vagueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rule that functions as a prior restraint must include 'narrow, objective, and definite standards' to guide application and avoid unconstitutional vagueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague or broad terms create arbitrary enforcement and chill speech (Reno, Forsyth County, Shuttlesworth precedents). Agencies must craft comments policies with concrete examples and standards to avoid creating prior restraints and to pass constitutional review.
